questions.q: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), what is the definitive weight threshold for a Low Birth Weight (LBW) infant measured within the first hour of life?
options: A) Less than 1000 grams
B) Less than 1500 grams
C) Less than 2500 grams
D) Less than 3000 grams
questions.hint: Less than 2500 g within the first hour of life.
questions.explanation: WHO defines a Low Birth Weight (LBW) baby as one with a birth weight of less than 2500 g (irrespective of gestational age), measured within the first hour of life before significant weight loss occurs.

questions.q: How does WHO classify an infant with a birth weight of less than 1000 grams?
options: A) Low Birth Weight (LBW)
B) Extremely Low Birth Weight (ELBW)
C) Very Low Birth Weight (VLBW)
D) Small for Gestational Age (SGA)
questions.hint: Birth weight < 1000 g is Extremely Low Birth Weight (ELBW).
questions.explanation: An infant born weighing less than 1000 g is categorized as Extremely Low Birth Weight (ELBW), whereas VLBW is 1000 g to <1500 g.

questions.q: What proportion of all low birth weight neonates worldwide is accounted for by Small for Date / Intrauterine Growth Restricted (SGA/IUGR) infants?
options: A) One-third (1/3)
B) One-half (1/2)
C) Two-thirds (2/3)
D) Three-quarters (3/4)
questions.hint: Two-thirds (2/3) of LBW infants globally are SGA/IUGR.
questions.explanation: Preterm birth accounts for approximately 1/3 of LBW infants, while intrauterine growth restriction (SGA/IUGR) accounts for 2/3 of LBW neonates globally.

questions.q: What is the defining gestational age limit for a Preterm infant according to WHO guidelines?
options: A) Delivery prior to 34 completed weeks of gestation
B) Delivery prior to 37 completed weeks of gestation
C) Delivery prior to 38 completed weeks of gestation
D) Delivery prior to 40 completed weeks of gestation
questions.hint: Prior to 37 completed weeks (<37 weeks).
questions.explanation: Prematurity is defined by gestational age at birth as any delivery occurring prior to 37 completed weeks (<37 weeks) of gestation.

questions.q: According to global WHO estimates, approximately how many Low Birth Weight babies are born each year, and what percentage of these births occurs in developing countries?
options: A) 5 million babies; 50% in developing countries
B) 10 million babies; 75% in developing countries
C) 25 million babies; nearly 95% in developing countries
D) 50 million babies; 30% in developing countries
questions.hint: About 25 million annually, with nearly 95% in developing countries.
questions.explanation: Global WHO estimates indicate ~25 million LBW babies are born annually (17% of all births), with nearly 95% born in developing countries.

questions.q: How is Small for Gestational Age (SGA) defined clinically on neonatal growth charts?
options: A) Birth weight below the 5th percentile for gestational age
B) Birth weight below the 10th percentile (or >2 SDs below the mean) for gestational age
C) Birth weight below the 25th percentile for gestational age
D) Birth weight below 2000 g regardless of percentile
questions.hint: Below the 10th percentile (or >2 SD below the mean) for gestational age.
questions.explanation: SGA is defined as an infant whose birth weight is less than the 10th percentile for gestational age or more than 2 standard deviations below the mean.

questions.q: What is the distinction between the terms 'Small for Gestational Age' (SGA) and 'Intrauterine Growth Restriction' (IUGR)?
options: A) SGA describes growth over time; IUGR describes weight at delivery
B) SGA is an obstetrician's ultrasound finding; IUGR is a pediatrician's birth label
C) SGA is used by pediatricians for a single point on a growth curve; IUGR is used by obstetricians for a pattern of growth over time
D) SGA applies only to post-term infants; IUGR applies only to preterms
questions.hint: SGA = single point on growth curve; IUGR = pattern of growth over time.
questions.explanation: SGA describes a static measurement at birth (<10th percentile), whereas IUGR describes a dynamic fetal growth restriction pattern observed over time in utero.

questions.q: What is the defining birth weight threshold for Macrosomia in a full-term infant?
options: A) Greater than 3500 g
B) Greater than 3800 g
C) Greater than 4000 g
D) Greater than 4500 g
questions.hint: Greater than 4000 g.
questions.explanation: Macrosomia is explicitly defined as a birth weight of greater than 4000 g in a term infant.

questions.q: What percentile threshold categorizes an infant as Large for Gestational Age (LGA)?
options: A) Weight > 75th percentile for gestational age
B) Weight > 80th percentile for gestational age
C) Weight > 90th percentile for gestational age
D) Weight > 95th percentile for gestational age
questions.hint: Above the 90th percentile for gestational age.
questions.explanation: LGA is defined as an infant whose birth weight is greater than the 90th percentile for their specific gestational age.

questions.q: Compared to normal birth weight infants, how much higher is the overall mortality rate in Low Birth Weight infants?
options: A) 2 times higher
B) 5 times higher
C) 10 times higher
D) 20 times higher
questions.hint: 20 times higher mortality rate.
questions.explanation: Mortality in low birth weight infants is reported to be 20 times higher than that of normal birth weight neonates.

questions.q: Under the WHO sub-classification of prematurity, how is an infant born at 29 weeks of gestation categorized?
options: A) Extremely preterm (<28 weeks)
B) Very preterm (28 0/7 to 31 6/7 weeks)
C) Moderate preterm (32 0/7 to 33 6/7 weeks)
D) Late preterm (34 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks)
questions.hint: 28 to 31 6/7 weeks is very preterm.
questions.explanation: WHO classifies preterm infants as Extremely preterm (<28 wks), Very preterm (28 to 31 6/7 wks), Moderate preterm (32 to 33 6/7 wks), and Late preterm (34 to 36 6/7 wks).

questions.q: What is the single highest risk factor in a patient's past obstetric history for spontaneous preterm delivery in a current pregnancy?
options: A) Prior cervical conization procedure
B) Prior dilation and curettage (D&C)
C) Prior preterm birth
D) History of uterine fibroids
questions.hint: A prior preterm birth is the strongest obstetric risk factor.
questions.explanation: A history of prior preterm birth is listed as the single highest risk factor for subsequent spontaneous premature delivery.

questions.q: Symmetric Intrauterine Growth Restriction (IUGR) typically begins early in gestation (1st trimester) during which cellular growth stage?
options: A) Stage I (Hyperplasia: rapid mitosis and increased DNA content)
B) Stage II (Hypertrophy alone)
C) Stage III (Fat and connective tissue accumulation)
D) Stage IV (Placental involution)
questions.hint: Stage I (hyperplasia) early in gestation.
questions.explanation: Symmetric IUGR results from early insult during Stage I (hyperplasia, 4–20 weeks), leading to an undersized fetus with fewer total cells of all types.

questions.q: Which clinical pattern distinguishes Asymmetric IUGR from Symmetric IUGR?
options: A) Weight, length, and head circumference are all equally reduced
B) Weight is predominantly reduced, with relative sparing of brain growth, head circumference, and long bones
C) Head circumference is severely reduced while body weight is completely preserved
D) Length is reduced while weight and head size are above the 90th percentile
questions.hint: Weight is mainly reduced while head circumference and length are relatively spared.
questions.explanation: Asymmetric growth restriction manifests late in gestation (2nd/3rd trimester), causing a reduction in cell size and fetal weight while relative brain growth and head circumference are spared.

questions.q: What maternal vascular condition is the most common cause of Asymmetric IUGR due to placental insufficiency in the third trimester?
options: A) First-trimester Cytomegalovirus infection
B) Maternal Preeclampsia / Hypertension
C) Chromosomal trisomy 21
D) Maternal hypothyroidism
questions.hint: Maternal preeclampsia or hypertension.
questions.explanation: Asymmetric IUGR typically arises late in pregnancy from uteroplacental insufficiency caused by maternal vascular diseases such as preeclampsia, hypertension, or long-standing diabetes.

questions.q: What classic congenital overgrowth syndrome presents with Macrosomia, Omphalocele, Macroglossia, ear creases, hemihypertrophy, and neonatal hypoglycemia?
options: A) WAGR syndrome
B) Silver-Russell syndrome
C) Denys-Drash syndrome
D) Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
questions.hint: Macrosomia, omphalocele, macroglossia, and hypoglycemia = Beckwith-Wiedemann.
questions.explanation: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a rare cause of macrosomia/LGA characterized by the classic presentation of macrosomia, omphalocele, macroglossia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

questions.q: What is the primary pathophysiological driver of fetal Macrosomia in an infant born to a diabetic mother?
options: A) Excess maternal thyroid hormone crossing the placenta
B) Anabolic effects of high fetal insulin levels produced in response to excessive maternal blood glucose
C) Fetal growth hormone hypersecretion triggered by maternal anemia
D) Placental synthesis of excessive glucagon
questions.hint: Fetal hyperinsulinemia driven by high maternal glucose.
questions.explanation: Maternal hyperglycemia leads to excessive fetal glucose transfer, inducing fetal pancreatic beta-cell hyperplasia and hyperinsulinism; fetal insulin acts as a potent anabolic growth hormone.

questions.q: Which anatomical structural birth defect is 2 to 3 times more likely to occur in infants of diabetic mothers due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid?
options: A) Tracheoesophageal fistula
B) Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
C) Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN)
D) Pulmonary sequestration
questions.hint: Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN).
questions.explanation: Transient tachypnea of the newborn is 2 to 3 times more common in infants of diabetic mothers because maternal hyperinsulinemia delays fetal lung fluid clearance.

questions.q: What specific skeletal structural defect is uniquely associated with maternal diabetes during early organogenesis?
options: A) Achondroplasia
B) Caudal Regression Syndrome (sacral agenesis)
C) Osteogenesis imperfecta
D) Radial ray aplasia
questions.hint: Caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis).
questions.explanation: Maternal hyperglycemia during organogenesis increases the risk of specific congenital anomalies, including Caudal Regression Syndrome, spina bifida, and heart defects.

questions.q: During what timeframe after delivery can the New Ballard Score be utilized to assess physical and neuromuscular gestational age maturity in a newborn?
options: A) Only within the first 15 minutes of life
B) Up to 4 days after birth (most practically used in the first 24 hours)
C) Between 7 and 14 days post-delivery
D) At 1 month of age
questions.hint: Up to 4 days after birth (commonly in the first 24 hours).
questions.explanation: The New Ballard Score evaluates neuromuscular and physical maturity parameters and can be validly performed up to 4 days after birth, though standard clinical practice applies it within the first 24 hours.

questions.q: What physical skin and neurological features are characteristic of a premature infant (<37 weeks) on physical examination?
options: A) Thick, leathery, cracked skin with prominent flexed posture
B) Thin, shiny, pink skin with easily visible underlying veins, minimal subcutaneous fat, and reduced spontaneous muscle tone
C) Deep plantar creases covering the entire sole with rigid recoil
D) Abundant ear cartilage with instant recoil and full nipple buds
questions.hint: Thin, shiny, pink skin with visible veins, little fat, and reduced tone.
questions.explanation: Preterm infants have thin, translucent, pink skin revealing underlying subcutaneous vessels, scarce fat/hair, soft ear pinnae, and hypotonic, extended posture.

questions.q: At what gestational age does the Moro reflex first appear, and when does it become fully established in the neonate?
options: A) Appears at 20 weeks; established at 24 weeks
B) Appears at 28 to 32 weeks; well established by 37 weeks
C) Appears at 35 weeks; established at 42 weeks
D) Appears only after term delivery
questions.hint: Starts around 28–32 weeks and is well established by 37 weeks.
questions.explanation: The Moro reflex begins between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation and becomes established by 37 weeks. Palmar grasp begins at 28 weeks (established at 32 weeks).

questions.q: Why are preterm infants exceptionally vulnerable to Hypothermia?
options: A) Excessive subcutaneous fat accumulation
B) High metabolic rate with shivering thermogenesis
C) Large body surface area to volume ratio, inadequate glycogen and fat stores, and poor muscle tone
D) Hyperkeratosis of the epidermis preventing heat transfer
questions.hint: High surface-area-to-volume ratio, low fat/glycogen stores, and poor tone.
questions.explanation: Preterm infants have a very high surface-area-to-mass ratio, thin skin, lack of insulating brown fat/glycogen, and poor flexion posture, accelerating radiant and evaporative heat loss.

questions.q: In the grading system for Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH) in preterm infants, what defines Grade IV IVH?
options: A) Hemorrhage confined strictly to the germinal matrix
B) Intraventricular hemorrhage without ventricular dilatation
C) Intraventricular hemorrhage with ventricular dilatation
D) Intraventricular hemorrhage with direct extension into the brain parenchyma
questions.hint: Extension of hemorrhage into the brain parenchyma.
questions.explanation: IVH grading: Grade I = germinal matrix alone; Grade II = IVH without dilatation; Grade III = IVH with ventricular dilatation; Grade IV = IVH extending into parenchymal tissue.

questions.q: What gestational age limit defines the threshold below which infants lack adequate coordination of sucking and swallowing reflexes, necessitating feeding via gavage or intravenously?
options: A) Born prior to 34 weeks of gestation
B) Born prior to 36 weeks of gestation
C) Born prior to 38 weeks of gestation
D) Born prior to 40 weeks of gestation
questions.hint: Before 34 weeks of gestation.
questions.explanation: Sucking and swallowing coordination is immature before 34 weeks of gestation; infants born <34 weeks require nasogastric/gavage or IV nutritional support.

questions.q: What classic triadic clinical presentation signals the onset of Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC), the most common surgical emergency in preterm infants?
options: A) High fever, bilious vomiting, and diarrhea
B) Bloody stools, feeding intolerance, and a distended, tender abdomen
C) Jaundice, hepatomegaly, and acholic stools
D) Scaphoid abdomen, cyanosis, and hematemesis
questions.hint: Feeding intolerance, distended/tender abdomen, and bloody stools.
questions.explanation: NEC classically manifests with feeding intolerance, abdominal distension/tenderness, and gross or microscopic blood in the stool, risking bowel perforation.

questions.q: What is the incidence rate of Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) in preterm infants weighing less than 1000 grams at birth?
options: A) Approximately 10%
B) Approximately 25%
C) Approximately 50%
D) Approximately 80%
questions.hint: Around 80% in infants <1000 g.
questions.explanation: The incidence of PDA increases with degree of prematurity; it occurs in ~50% of infants <1750 g and approximately 80% of infants weighing <1000 g.

questions.q: Why are sick, small preterm infants at risk for Chronic Bilirubin Encephalopathy (Kernicterus) at serum bilirubin levels as low as 10 mg/dL (170 µmol/L)?
options: A) Increased serum albumin binding capacity
B) Enhanced blood-brain barrier tightness
C) Immature liver conjugation, reduced serum albumin binding, and increased blood-brain barrier permeability
D) Absence of enterohepatic circulation
questions.hint: Immature conjugation, lower albumin binding, and more permeable blood-brain barrier.
questions.explanation: Preterm infants have lower albumin levels, weaker albumin binding, and an immature blood-brain barrier, predisposing them to bilirubin toxicity at lower thresholds (e.g., 10 mg/dL).

questions.q: Why is routine L-thyroxine treatment NOT recommended for Transient Hypothyroxinemia of Prematurity in extremely preterm infants?
options: A) Because TSH is markedly elevated >100 mIU/L
B) Because transient hypothyroxinemia features low T4 with normal TSH due to immature hypothalamic-pituitary axis and thyroid hormone replacement has proven not beneficial
C) Because L-thyroxine causes immediate closure of the fontanelle
D) Because it causes severe renal sodium retention
questions.hint: Low T4 with normal TSH; replacement has not shown clinical benefit.
questions.explanation: Extremely preterm infants frequently exhibit low T4 with normal TSH (transient hypothyroxinemia); clinical trials show L-thyroxine supplementation provides no therapeutic benefit.

questions.q: What major intrapartum mechanical complication causes high rates of Perinatal Asphyxia in SGA/IUGR fetuses during labor?
options: A) Rupture of the fetal membranes at 20 weeks
B) Compression of maternal spiral arteries during uterine contractions causing transient cessation of marginally adequate placental blood flow
C) Rapid expansion of the fetal head
D) Sudden closure of the ductus venosus
questions.hint: Contractions compress spiral arteries, further reducing marginal placental flow.
questions.explanation: SGA fetuses with chronic placental insufficiency have minimal respiratory reserve; each uterine contraction compresses spiral arteries, further reducing blood flow and precipitating asphyxia.

questions.q: What is the target normal core body temperature range that must be maintained during thermal regulation of a Low Birth Weight infant?
questions.explanation: Non-pharmacological thermal management requires maintaining the neonate's body temperature strictly between 36.5°C and 37.5°C.

questions.q: Where should the skin temperature probe of a servo-controlled radiant warmer be positioned on a low birth weight neonate?
options: A) Over the interscapular brown fat area
B) Over the right upper abdomen, approximately 3 cm below the right costal margin
C) Over the anterior mid-thigh
D) Over the left parietal bone of the skull
questions.hint: Right upper abdomen, ~3 cm below the right costal margin.
questions.explanation: Guidelines state that the temperature probe for servo-mode radiant warmers must be placed over the right side of the abdomen, ~3 cm below the right costal margin.

questions.q: At what controlled rate should a hypothermic low birth weight neonate be rewarmed to prevent rewarming-induced complications such as apnea or hypotension?
options: A) 0.1°C per hour
B) 0.5°C per hour
C) 2.0°C per hour
D) 5.0°C per hour
questions.hint: 0.5°C per hour.
questions.explanation: Hypothermic neonates must be rewarmed slowly at a rate of 0.5°C per hour to avoid rapid vasodilation, hypotension, and apnea.

questions.q: What ambient nursery room temperature range is recommended to support thermal balance for low birth weight infants?
options: A) 18°C to 20°C
B) 21°C to 24°C
C) 25°C to 28°C
D) 30°C to 35°C
questions.explanation: Room temperature for LBW infant care areas should be maintained between 25°C and 28°C.

questions.q: What initial enteral feeding strategy is recommended to prime the immature gut in stable low birth weight neonates?
options: A) High-volume full-strength formula on Day 1
B) Minimal Enteral Feeding (MEF / trophic feeds)
C) Hypertonic dextrose via bolus
D) Complete enteral starvation for 14 days
questions.hint: Minimal enteral feeding (MEF / trophic feeds).
questions.explanation: Non-pharmacological feeding protocols initiate Minimal Enteral Feeding (MEF or trophic feeds) to stimulate gut maturation before gradually advancing fluid volumes.

questions.q: What daily caloric requirement and expected daily weight gain are targeted for growing preterm infants?
options: A) 80 kcal/kg/day; expected weight gain 5 g/day
B) 120 kcal/kg/day; expected weight gain 10 to 30 g/day
C) 180 kcal/kg/day; expected weight gain 50 g/day
D) 200 kcal/kg/day; expected weight gain 100 g/day
questions.hint: 120 kcal/kg/day and 10–30 g/day weight gain.
questions.explanation: Nutritional targets for preterm management require a caloric intake of 120 kcal/kg/day, aiming for an average weight gain of 10 to 30 g/day.

questions.q: What standard empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen is recommended for suspected neonatal sepsis in low birth weight infants, and what is its typical duration?
options: A) Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin for 14 days
B) Ampicillin + Gentamicin for 5 to 7 days
C) Ciprofloxacin + Metronidazole for 10 days
D) Erythromycin monotherapy for 3 days
questions.hint: Ampicillin + gentamicin for 5 to 7 days.
questions.explanation: Empirical pharmacological treatment for suspected early neonatal sepsis consists of Ampicillin plus Gentamicin for 5 to 7 days, adjusted by clinical response and cultures.

questions.q: Why must unfortified human breast milk be fortified with multicomponent human milk fortifier when fed to growing VLBW/ELBW infants?
options: A) Human milk lacks sufficient protein, calcium, and phosphorus to meet high metabolic demands and prevent Osteopenia of Prematurity
B) Human milk causes severe hypernatremia
C) Human milk contains excessive vitamin D that inhibits gut absorption
D) Human milk prevents gastric emptying
questions.hint: Needs extra protein, calcium, and phosphorus to support growth and bone mineralization.
questions.explanation: Human milk provides inadequate calcium, phosphorus, and protein for very low birth weight infants; fortification is essential to support bone mineralization and prevent osteopenia.

questions.q: Why does Polycythemia develop in SGA infants affected by chronic in utero hypoxia from placental insufficiency?
options: A) Decreased fetal renal breakdown of hemoglobin
B) Chronic hypoxemia stimulates fetal erythropoietin release, driving increased erythrocyte production
C) Hyperinsulinemia directly inhibits red cell destruction in the spleen
D) Maternal red cells cross the placenta into the fetal circulation
questions.hint: Chronic hypoxia increases fetal erythropoietin production.
questions.explanation: Placental insufficiency causes chronic mild fetal hypoxia, which triggers erythropoietin surge and polycythemia (hyperviscosity), presenting at birth as a ruddy appearance.

questions.q: At what serum calcium threshold (or clinical presentation) is active medical intervention required for neonatal hypocalcemia?
options: A) Calcium < 3.0 mmol/L in all infants
B) Symptomatic Hypocalcemia or total serum calcium < 7 mg/dL (<1.75 mmol/L) / ionized calcium < 4 mg/dL (<1 mmol/L)
C) Calcium < 2.5 mmol/L with normal glucose
D) Calcium > 12 mg/dL only
questions.hint: Symptomatic or total Ca < 7 mg/dL (<1.75 mmol/L) / ionized Ca < 4 mg/dL (<1 mmol/L).
questions.explanation: Hypocalcemia treatment (IV calcium gluconate) is indicated if clinical symptoms (jitteriness, seizures, apnea) occur or total calcium drops <7 mg/dL (ionized <4 mg/dL / <1 mmol/L).

questions.q: A neonate born at 26 weeks (birth weight 850 g) has grunting, retractions, cyanosis, and nasal flaring at 15 minutes, with a reticulogranular ('ground-glass') chest X-ray and air bronchograms. Identify the pulmonary condition, biochemical deficiency, and definitive therapy.
options: A) Meconium Aspiration Syndrome; Lack of alveolar macrophages; Endotracheal suctioning alone
B) Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS); Deficiency of alveolar Surfactant leading to alveolar collapse; Administer exogenous surfactant via endotracheal tube and provide CPAP/assisted ventilation
C) Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn; Delayed fluid clearance; Diuretics
D) Congenital Pneumonia; Group B Streptococcus; Inhaled nitric oxide alone
questions.hint: Extreme prematurity + ground-glass CXR = RDS (surfactant deficiency); treat with surfactant and CPAP/ventilation.
questions.explanation: Prematurity (<28 wks) with ground-glass CXR indicates RDS caused by surfactant deficiency. Treatment requires exogenous surfactant replacement and mechanical ventilation/CPAP.

questions.q: A 2-day-old preterm infant (1100 g) on enteral feeds develops abdominal distension, lethargy, temperature instability, gross bloody stool, and pneumatosis intestinalis on X-ray. What is the diagnosis, main surgical risk, and immediate management?
options: A) Intussusception; Bowel gangrene; Perform air enema reduction
B) Hirschsprung's disease; Toxic megacolon; Rectal biopsy

C) Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC); Intestinal perforation with pneumoperitoneum; Stop enteral feeds (NPO), insert NG tube for decompression, start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and obtain surgical consult
D) Meconium Ileus; Volvulus; Administer N-acetylcysteine enema
questions.hint: Pneumatosis intestinalis + bloody stools + distension = NEC; watch for perforation; NPO, NG decompression, IV antibiotics, surgery consult.
questions.explanation: Abdominal distension, bloody stools, and pneumatosis intestinalis define NEC. Key risk is bowel perforation. Management includes NPO, NG decompression, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and surgical evaluation.

questions.q: A term neonate (4600 g) born after difficult delivery to a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes is listless, ruddy, and jittery at 2 hours with blood glucose 1.2 mmol/L. Diagnose the metabolic problem, why it happened after birth, and what birth trauma to check for.
options: A) Congenital Hypothyroidism; Absence of thyroid stimulation; Check for congenital dislocation of hip

B) Neonatal Hypoglycemia secondary to hyperinsulinemia; Sudden termination of maternal glucose delivery upon cord clamping while fetal insulin levels remain high; Examine for clavicular fracture and brachial plexus injury (shoulder dystocia)
C) Hypocalcemia; Calcitonin surge; Check for skull fracture
D) Galactosemia; Enzyme defect; Check for cataract
questions.hint: Maternal DM + macrosomia + low glucose after cord clamping = hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia; check clavicle/brachial plexus.
questions.explanation: Maternal DM causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, which rapidly drives down glucose when maternal supply ends at cord clamping (hypoglycemia). Macrosomia causes shoulder dystocia, risking clavicular fracture or Erb's palsy.

questions.q: An infant born at 38 weeks weighs 1800 g (<3rd percentile) with a disproportionately large head, wizened facies, loose skin, thin cord, and length/head circumference at the 35th percentile. Classify the IUGR pattern, timing/cause, and expected birth complications.
options: A) Symmetric IUGR; 1st trimester TORCH infection; Thrombocytopenia and hypercalcemia
B) Asymmetric IUGR; 3rd trimester placental insufficiency (e.g., preeclampsia); Hypoglycemia (depleted glycogen stores) and Polycythemia (chronic hypoxia)
C) Normal term infant; Genetic dwarfism; Leukocytosis
D) Large for Gestational Age; Maternal diabetes; Hyperglycemia
questions.hint: Head/length spared + low weight = asymmetric IUGR (late placental insufficiency); watch for hypoglycemia and polycythemia.
questions.explanation: Disproportionate weight reduction with head/length sparing indicates Asymmetric IUGR from late placental insufficiency. Complications include hypoglycemia (low glycogen) and polycythemia (EPO surge from hypoxia).

questions.q: A 28-week preterm infant on a ventilator suddenly drops hematocrit at day 4 with a bulging fontanelle, apnea, and bradycardia; cranial ultrasound shows lateral ventricular blood, ventricular dilation, and parenchymal extension. Diagnose and grade it, name the source of bleeding, and state the long-term risk.
options: A) Subdural hematoma; Sagittal sinus; Microcephaly
B) Intraventricular Hemorrhage (Grade IV); Delicate unsupported capillaries of the Germinal Matrix; Cerebral palsy and neurodevelopmental delay
C) Epidural hematoma; Middle meningeal artery; Hydrocephalus alone
D) Subarachnoid hemorrhage; Circle of Willis; Complete recovery without sequelae
questions.hint: IVH with parenchymal extension = Grade IV from germinal matrix capillaries; risk of cerebral palsy.
questions.explanation: Sudden drop in Hct, bulging fontanelle, and parenchymal extension define Grade IV IVH, arising from rupture of fragile germinal matrix capillaries. White matter injury predisposes to cerebral palsy.

questions.q: A 39-week infant of a preeclamptic mother passes thick meconium during distressed labor and is limp, cyanotic, and gasping at birth. What caused in utero meconium passage/gasping, what syndrome is likely, and why is it worse in SGA/IUGR?
options: A) Fetal hyperinsulinemia; TTN; Reduced chest wall compliance
B) Intrapartum Perinatal Asphyxia; Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS); Meconium is suspended in a smaller, oligohydramnic volume of amniotic fluid, making it highly concentrated
C) Congenital sepsis; RDS; Absence of alveolar surfactant
D) Diaphragmatic hernia; Pneumothorax; Hypoplastic lungs
questions.hint: Intrapartum asphyxia -> MAS; more concentrated in reduced amniotic fluid.
questions.explanation: Intrapartum asphyxia triggers gasping and meconium passage; aspiration causes MAS. MAS is severe in IUGR because meconium is concentrated in reduced amniotic fluid.

questions.q: A 37-week infant of a diabetic mother has jitteriness, twitching, and apnea at 18 hours with normal glucose (3.8 mmol/L), total Ca 1.4 mmol/L, and Mg 0.4 mmol/L; IV calcium infusion fails to stop twitching. Why did calcium fail, and what must be corrected first?
options: A) Calcium was inactivated by glucose; Give oral Vitamin D
B) Hypomagnesemia impairs Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) secretion and organ responsiveness; Hypomagnesemia must be corrected first for hypocalcemia to resolve
C) Calcium was excreted by the liver; Give IV furosemide
D) High insulin blocked calcium uptake; Give IV glucagon
questions.hint: Low magnesium impairs PTH secretion/response; correct hypomagnesemia first.
questions.explanation: Hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and action; recalcitrant hypocalcemia in infants of diabetic mothers will not respond to calcium until magnesium is corrected.

questions.q: A 30-week preterm infant (1250 g) on unfortified breast milk and chronic furosemide has craniotabes, rib beading, high alkaline phosphatase, and bone thinning at 8 weeks. What condition is this, what are the dietary/drug causes, and how is it prevented?
options: A) Osteoperosis; Excessive vitamin A; Give high-dose calcitonin

B) Osteopenia of Prematurity (Metabolic Bone Disease); Inadequate intake of Calcium/Phosphorus/Vit D in unfortified human milk, exacerbated by renal calcium loss from Furosemide; Fortify human milk and provide Vitamin D supplementation
C) Osteopetrosis; High calcium intake; Stop all milk feeds
D) Achondroplasia; Genetic mutation; Surgical alignment
questions.hint: Osteopenia of prematurity from Ca/PO4/Vit D deficiency + furosemide; prevent with milk fortification and vitamin D.
questions.explanation: High alk phos and bone thinning indicate Osteopenia of Prematurity from calcium/phosphorus deficiency in unfortified milk, aggravated by loop diuretics. Prevention requires milk fortification and vitamin D.

questions.q: Comparing a Preterm LBW infant vs a Term SGA infant: which is mainly at risk for immaturity complications (RDS, IVH, ROP, NEC, hyperbilirubinemia, PDA), and which is mainly at risk for chronic in utero hypoxia complications (asphyxia, MAS, polycythemia, hypoglycemia)?
options: A) 1. Term SGA infant; 2. Preterm LBW infant
B) 1. Preterm LBW infant; 2. Term SGA / IUGR infant
C) 1. LGA infant; 2. Preterm LBW infant
D) Both infants have identical complication profiles
questions.hint: 1. Preterm LBW infant; 2. Term SGA / IUGR infant.
questions.explanation: Preterm infants suffer complications of organ system immaturity (RDS, IVH, NEC, ROP, PDA). Term SGA infants suffer complications of intrauterine stress/hypoxia (asphyxia, MAS, polycythemia, hypoglycemia).

questions.q: For a 1200 g VLBW infant in the NICU: what immediate thermal/non-drug care is needed, what screening tests are mandatory, and what empirical antibiotics cover suspected sepsis?
options: A) 1. Place in open crib; 2. Gastric lavage; 3. Oral erythromycin

B) 1. Servo-controlled radiant warmer/incubator (target temp 36.5–37.5°C), Minimal Enteral Feeding, KMC; 2. Pulse oximetry, blood gas/lactate, Bilirubin, Cranial Ultrasound (for IVH), ROP eye exam (at 31–33 wks), Screening for Osteopenia (Ca/Phos/AlkPhos); 3. IV Ampicillin + Gentamicin for 5–7 days
C) 1. Cold bath to reduce metabolism; 2. CT scan of abdomen; 3. IV Vancomycin alone
D) 1. Immediate discharge home; 2. No testing needed; 3. No antibiotics
questions.hint: Warmer/incubator (36.5–37.5°C) + MEF/KMC; cranial US, ROP, osteopenia screen; ampicillin + gentamicin.
questions.explanation: Comprehensive management of VLBW neonates involves strict thermoregulation (36.5–37.5°C) and minimal enteral feeds, routine screening for IVH (cranial US), ROP, and osteopenia, and empirical Ampicillin + Gentamicin for suspected sepsis.
